summary: This work develops an information-theoretic framework to quantify how error-syndrome information improves logical observable estimation in fault-tolerant quantum computing. The key finding is a sharp separation: classical syndrome-aware protocols (fixed measurement basis) can improve effective logical error rates by at most a factor of two on average, but quantum syndrome-aware protocols (adaptive measurement basis) can achieve exponentially smaller error rates with multiple code blocks.
motivation: Early fault-tolerant devices will retain residual logical errors after error correction, requiring estimation of logical observables from noisy states. While syndrome information is routinely discarded after decoding, recent work suggests it could improve performance, but fundamental limits on this utility remain unclear.
method: Using quantum estimation theory and Fisher information analysis, the authors compare three protocols: syndrome-agnostic (no syndrome use), classical syndrome-aware (syndrome-conditioned classical post-processing only), and quantum syndrome-aware (syndrome-conditioned quantum measurements). They derive universal bounds via the convexity of the Fisher information function and prove exponential suppression through entanglement-assisted recovery exploiting information correlation between damaged and intact code blocks.
result: For classical protocols, Theorem 1 proves the effective logical error rate satisfies $(1-\theta_i^2)/2 \cdot \epsilon_i \leq \epsilon_i^\mathrm{cSynd} \leq \epsilon_i$ on average, implying at most quadratic sampling improvement. For quantum protocols, Theorem 2 demonstrates that with $m$ code blocks of even-distance codes, $\mathbb{E}_\mathrm{Haar}[\epsilon_i^\mathrm{qSynd}]/\epsilon_i = O(2^{-k'\,m})$ in the low-noise limit, achieving exponential advantage. Numerical results on surface and repetition codes validate these conclusions.
